source.title: Minor interpretability exploration #3: Extending superposition to different activation functions (loss landscape)

record.tranche_reason: The author reran the TMS toy-model code and measurements while changing the activation function, reporting superposition and loss-landscape results.
record.gate_note: The post reports qualitative comparisons and aggregate loss ranges, but not per-activation numerical tables in the text. It mentions notebooks, graphs and tables in an external folder; those contents are not part of the supplied text. Excludes cited results from prior work.
record.test_reason: The post varies the output activation in the Timaeus TMS toy autoencoders and reports qualitative degree of superposition, loss and LLC. In this setup the hidden layer is a linear bottleneck with no privileged basis, so there are no neurons whose polysemanticity could be measured. Feature superposition geometry is a related but different construct from the share of polysemantic neurons that V5 names. The post also never tests whether superposition causes polysemantic neurons (V3). Its results therefore go under fits_no_version, not version verdicts.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right but incomplete. The author concludes that more superposition gives marginally smaller losses, and that superposition develops after the initial large loss drop, during phase changes. Sharp, non-negative, asymmetric activation functions gave the most superposition and lowest losses. The bounded-function and SoLU results are confusing and need more research.
record.recipe_differences: The TMS notebook and original code were reused, with activation functions changed. The author describes the setup as autoencoders; the post does not specify exact model dimensions or provide the underlying tabular results in its text.
record.method_sensitivity: Activation function; the author also notes lack of LayerNorm as a possible factor in the SoLU result.

fits_no_version.finding: In TMS toy autoencoders, the output activation function strongly changes the degree of feature superposition. Small changes (CELU vs GELU) give large differences, while loss and LLC differ little.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The degree of feature superposition in toy models depends strongly on activation-function shape, e.g. sharp, non-negative or asymmetric versus bounded or capped functions.

fits_no_version.finding: Without LayerNorm, SoLU gave more superposition than softmax in the TMS autoencoder, contrary to SoLU's design aim.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SoLU does not reduce superposition in toy autoencoders without LayerNorm.

fits_no_version.finding: More superposition reduced loss by at most one order of magnitude, with no correlation beyond a threshold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Superposition yields only marginal loss benefits in toy models.

record.problems: The author characterizes the exploration as small, low-stakes and without prior predictions. The supplied text gives qualitative findings rather than per-activation numbers, uncertainty estimates or a performance evaluation; it notes possible model differences and lack of LayerNorm as explanations requiring further research.

untested.parts: No language models or MLP neurons.
No test of whether superposition causes polysemantic neurons; sparsity and capacity are not varied.
No initialization, regularization or noise manipulations.

Varies activation functions but measures superposition in a basis-free hidden layer, not the share of polysemantic neurons. No architecture or regularization variations and no task-performance trade-off on neuron polysemanticity.

missing.what: Superposition emerges only after the largest loss drops and coincides with phase changes (small loss drops, LLC rises). Low superposition also forms more slowly.

record.verdict_notes: The record treats superposition degree as a proxy for polysemantic neuron share. In the TMS autoencoder the hidden layer has no activation and no privileged basis, so neuron polysemanticity is undefined there. I therefore reclassified the study as related-construct and gave no V5 verdict. The results are qualitative only, with tables in an external folder. The study is a LessWrong exploratory post.

versions.untested_parts: No image classifier neurons or visual inputs are examined.
No transformer language models, MLP neurons in language models, tokens or language-model contexts are examined.
The post studies superposition in toy models but does not test whether feature sparsity or a feature-to-neuron capacity ratio causes polysemanticity.
No test of initialization, regularization or training noise as causes of polysemantic neurons without capacity pressure.

Measures superposition in toy autoencoders rather than the share of polysemantic neurons in trained networks. Does not test modern convnets or regularization, and does not establish changes in task performance.
No neuron interpretations or tests of whether apparently unrelated inputs share a feature.
No comparison of activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.
